meta.title: Check your understanding: The photovoltaic effect

objectives: Explain why a photon's energy, not the brightness of the light, decides whether it can free an electron
Calculate a photon's energy from its wavelength with E ≈ 1240 ÷ λ, and how much of it is lost as heat
Compare the photoelectric effect with the photovoltaic effect

questions.prompt: Silicon has a band gap of 1.12 eV. Infrared light of wavelength 1300 nm shines on it, and then the beam is made ten times brighter. What happens?
choices: Ten times as many electron–hole pairs form, so the current rises tenfold
Each photon now carries ten times the energy, so it clears the gap
Still no pairs: each 0.95 eV photon is below the gap, however many arrive
A few pairs form, because two photons can add their energies together
questions.explain: Each photon carries 1240 ÷ 1300 ≈ 0.95 eV, less than 1.12 eV, and a photon hands over all its energy or none of it. Brighter light means more photons, not bigger ones, so the light still passes straight through.

questions.prompt: A violet photon of wavelength 400 nm is absorbed in silicon (band gap 1.12 eV). Roughly how much of its energy is lost as heat?
questions.explain: The photon carries 1240 ÷ 400 ≈ 3.10 eV. The electron keeps only the 1.12 eV of the gap and shakes off the surplus, 3.10 − 1.12 ≈ 1.98 eV, as heat (thermalisation). That is more than half of the photon's energy, not all of it.

questions.prompt: In the photovoltaic effect, where does the electron that a photon frees end up?
choices: Out of the material, collected by a separate electrode
Back in the same bond, giving off a photon of the same colour
In the valence band, leaving a hole in the conduction band
Still inside the material, lifted into the conduction band
questions.explain: In a solar cell the electron stays inside, raised from the valence band to the conduction band, and a built-in field then drives it round a circuit. Leaving the material altogether is the photoelectric effect, its cousin, whose threshold is the work function rather than the band gap.

questions.prompt: A green 500 nm photon carries 2.48 eV, more than twice silicon's 1.12 eV gap. In an ordinary silicon cell, how many electron–hole pairs can it make?
choices: Two, because it carries enough energy for two gap crossings
One, and the surplus 1.36 eV becomes heat
None, because its energy does not match the gap exactly
Two, but only when the light is very bright
questions.explain: In an ordinary cell one photon makes at most one pair: the electron lands high in the conduction band and quickly sheds the extra 1.36 eV as crystal vibrations. Turning that surplus into a second pair is still active research. The photon only has to reach the gap, not match it exactly.
